Empirical Research Plan  
“How does the venture-capital (VC) cycle influence the financing and subsequent performance of start-ups?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Preferred strategy: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variables (IV) design.

Why IV?  
• The amount of VC financing received by a firm is clearly endogenous: better ideas attract more money, and money in turn affects performance.  
• The VC industry is highly cyclical and its funding cycles are largely driven by shocks that are plausibly exogenous to any individual start-up (e.g., public-equity market run-ups that boost limited partners’ wealth, regulatory changes affecting pension-fund allocations).  
• Aggregate VC-supply shocks give us a powerful time-series shifter that can be interacted with cross-sectional exposure to generate firm-level quasi-random variation.

Concrete instrument (“supply-pull”):  
Z_it = (Capital Committed to New VC Funds in year t-1 / GDP_t-1)  
         × IndustryExposure_i  

IndustryExposure_i = share of the firm’s 3-digit SIC industry in total VC investments during the pre-sample period (1980-1982).  
The resulting shift-share instrument varies both over time and across firms.

Stage 1: ln(1+VCAmount_it) = α + β·Z_it + γ·X_it + η_i + τ_t + ε_it  
Stage 2: Performance_it = θ + δ·ln(1+ŴVCAmount_it) + λ·X_it + η_i + τ_t + u_it  

η_i – start-up fixed effects (or founder fixed effects for robustness)  
τ_t – calendar-year fixed effects (absorb macro trends)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable: ln(1 + VC dollars raised by start-up i in year t) or a dummy HighVC_it = 1 if firm raises ≥ median dollars in that calendar year.

Control: Firms that receive little or no VC in the same year, whose potential funding is nevertheless affected by the same macro VC-supply shock but that ended up “untreated.”

Treatment timing: The year in which a start-up closes its first VC round (t = 0). We follow each cohort for up to 10 years.

No running variable (not RDD).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Instrument relevance: VC fund-raising booms must translate into more money flowing to start-ups in industries that historically receive a lot of VC.  
  Plausibility: Industry-level evidence (NVCA, PitchBook) shows exactly this pattern.

A2. Exclusion: Conditional on year and industry fixed effects, the instrument affects a given start-up’s ex-post performance only through the additional VC dollars it enables, not through any direct channel.  
  Plausibility: Limited-partner wealth shocks (e.g., pension-fund or endowment portfolio returns) are unlikely to be correlated with the idiosyncratic future performance of any single young firm once we net out macro conditions.

A3. Monotonicity/No-defiers: A positive shock to VC supply cannot reduce the VC a firm receives.  
  Plausibility: More money never makes it harder to raise money.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): One firm’s funding shock does not directly change another sampled firm’s outcome except through equilibrium effects already captured by year fixed effects (we test robustness using state-by-year fixed effects).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Omitted macro shocks that jointly affect VC supply and start-up performance (e.g., tech bubbles).  
  Mitigation: Year fixed effects, industry-year fixed effects, control for NASDAQ returns and GDP growth; robustness with state-year FE.

T2. Direct effect of public-equity valuations on exit valuations (violating exclusion).  
  Mitigation: Use lagged VC-supply (t-1) instead of contemporaneous; perform placebo tests on pre-funding performance variables; alternative instrument using state-pension funding-ratio shocks that are unrelated to tech valuations.

T3. Measurement error in VC amounts (attenuates 2SLS power).  
  Mitigation: Use multiple sources (VentureXpert, PitchBook, SEC Form D) and instrument only the intensive margin (> $1 m); cluster SE at the founding cohort to avoid overstating precision.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast felm/iv
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# 1. Data Loading ---------------------------------------------------
vc  <- fread("startup_vc_data.csv")        # firm-year observations
funds <- fread("vc_fundraising.csv")       # industry aggregate
macro <- fread("macro_controls.csv")       # GDP, Nasdaq, etc.

# 2. Merge & Variable Construction ---------------------------------
dt <- merge(vc, funds, by = "year")
dt <- merge(dt, macro, by = "year")

# Shift-share instrument
# Pre-sample industry shares computed separately and merged in as ind_share
dt[, Z := (vc_funds_gdp) * ind_share]            # instrument
dt[, ln_vc := log1p(vc_amount)]                  # treatment
dt[, post_0 := year - first_vc_year]             # relative time

# 3. Baseline 2SLS --------------------------------------------------
iv_eq <- feols(performance_metric ~ 1 | ln_vc ~ Z,
               data = dt,
               fixef = ~ firm_id + year,
               cluster = ~ firm_id)

summary(iv_eq, cluster = "firm_id")

# 4. Robustness: leave-one-industry-out instrument -----------------
for(ind in unique(dt$industry3d)){
  res <- feols(performance_metric ~ 1 | ln_vc ~ Z,
               data = dt[industry3d != ind],
               fixef = ~ firm_id + year,
               cluster = ~ firm_id)
  cat(ind, coef(res, "ln_vc"), "\n")
}

# 5. Event-study graph as placebo ----------------------------------
evt <- feols(performance_metric ~ i(post_0, treated=ln_vc>0) + ln_vc,
             data = dt[abs(post_0)<=5],
             fixef = ~ firm_id + cohort_year)

iplot(evt)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts that greater VC availability relaxes financing constraints, allowing start-ups to scale faster and survive longer. I expect:  
• δ > 0 (positive causal effect).  
• Magnitude: A one-standard-deviation increase in ln(VC dollars) (~1.2 log points, ≈ ×3 money) raises 5-year employment by ≈ 20 % and revenue by ≈ 25 %.  
• Heterogeneity: Stronger effects for R&D-intensive and younger firms.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
C1 Instrument relevance ……………… 1  
C2 Instrument exogeneity …………… 0.5  
C3 Monotonicity / No defiers ……… 1  
C4 SUTVA …………………………………… 0.5  
C5 Robust standard errors / F-stat  1  

Overall: 4/5 items reasonably satisfied; main concern is exclusion/SUTVA, which we probe extensively with robustness and placebo tests.
